extracted.intended_audience: writers of memoir and creative-writing students (memoir workshop participants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for mining, testing, and shaping personal memory into memoir—techniques for excavating sensory moments, verifying recollection, assembling scenes, and avoiding memory pitfalls. Aimed at writers working from their own past.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-image sensory anchor
rubrics_metrics.description: “A single image can split open the hard seed of the past.” Use a sensory image (smell, sight, a photograph) as an entry point that can open and summon surrounding memories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a whiff of cumin conjures a father’s curry; a snapshot can trigger clothing, location, sequence. Treat images as triggers to follow other associative memories; cultivate and record those images first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro-excavation: start with a tiny instant
rubrics_metrics.description: “You start with a clear fix on a tiny instant, and pick at every knot until a thin thread comes undone that you can follow back through the mind’s labyrinth to other places.” Begin with a small, specific moment and probe its details to unlock larger sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: focus narrowly on one brief instant, interrogate sensory, spatial, emotional particulars, then follow the thread outward. This is a deliberate, iterative excavation rather than relying on broad summary memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow associative chains to rebuild context
rubrics_metrics.description: Memories often return as chains of association (people, places, classes, smells) that reveal context: e.g., remembering who sat behind you, then locker location, then route home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use associative linking—ask what came before/after, who else was present, what objects or routines anchored the moment—to reconstruct scene and sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept and collect fragmentary memories
rubrics_metrics.description: “Memory is a pinball in a machine—it messily ricochets around between image, idea, fragments of scenes...”—expect memory to be fragmented and nonlinear and gather those fragments rather than forcing linearity prematurely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep fragments (images, phrases, gestures) in your notes; later you can assemble or layer them into scenes. Avoid dismissing fragments as unusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism and verification of recollection
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t assume memory accuracy—test and corroborate recollections; immediate recordings often reveal mistakes. The author stages exercises showing that even smart witnesses err.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods: record right after events, compare accounts among witnesses, fact-check dates/times/objects. Use corroboration (documents, tapes, other people's accounts) to build an agreed-on version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of memory contamination and implanted details
rubrics_metrics.description: Memories can be altered by suggestion—researcher/author interventions can implant false facts (the author demonstrates adding a bracelet that the person doesn’t wear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: leading questions, rehearsing a version that introduces new elements. Be cautious when testing or persuading others—don’t inadvertently create false memories; treat newly suggested details as suspect until corroborated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose memories with narrative traction
rubrics_metrics.description: Some memories are 'useful' because they 'gain enough traction to haul you through the past'—select moments that open pathways to other material and can carry narrative weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer memories that lead to further scenes, character revelation, or causal/emotional development rather than isolated vignettes that don’t connect to a larger arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise, concrete sensory and physical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifics (colors, clothing, objects, timings) give credibility and vividness—examples include khaki vs. denim, black Nikes double-knotted, color of socks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect tactile, visual, auditory specifics when possible. Note that inaccurate specifics (especially time intervals) are common memory errors, so verify where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize variability in memory accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people have 'photographic recall' (memory aces) and get facts and dialogue spot on; most do not—memory clarity varies across individuals and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat exceptional-seeming recollections with interest but still verify; avoid generalizing about your or others' accuracy from one instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in reproducing dialogue and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Class exercises reveal mistakes in quoted dialogue and interpretative errors; the author corrects dialogue and interpretation on the board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing remembered dialogue, label uncertain lines, corroborate with recordings or witnesses when possible, and be mindful of conflating memory with later interpretation—distinguish what was said from how you now interpret it.
